epithet: Sayf Allah al-Maslul (The Unsheathed Sword of Allah)
role: Supreme Commander of Muslim forces under Abu Bakr
Leading military commander under the Prophet ﷺ and the first two Caliphs
summary: Khalid ibn al-Walid (RA) was the greatest military commander produced by the early Muslim community, earning from the Prophet ﷺ himself the title 'Sayf Allah al-Maslul' — the Unsheathed Sword of Allah. In a military career spanning the final campaigns of the Prophet ﷺ through the caliphates of Abu Bakr and Umar, he remained undefeated in over a hundred engagements and was the central figure in the rapid early Islamic conquests of Arabia, Persia, and Syria.
biography:
Khalid ibn al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah al-Makhzumi al-Qurashi was born around 585 CE in Makkah into the Banu Makhzum clan of Quraysh — a clan renowned for its warriors and horsemen. His father al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah was one of the wealthiest and most prominent men of Quraysh, a leader whose significance the Quran itself references (Surah al-Muddaththir, 74:11). Khalid grew up in an environment that prized martial excellence, and he developed into an exceptional horseman, swordsman, and military tactician from a young age.

Before his acceptance of Islam, Khalid was among the most formidable enemies the Muslim army faced. At the Battle of Uhud (3 AH / 625 CE), it was Khalid who led the Qurayshi cavalry around the right flank of the Muslim position — exploiting the gap left when the archers on the hillside abandoned their posts against the Prophet's explicit orders — and turned a Muslim near-victory into a devastating reversal. The Quraysh cavalry's flanking maneuver caused significant casualties among the Muslims and injured the Prophet ﷺ. Classical military historians have regarded this as one of the most tactically significant cavalry actions of the early Islamic period. The Muslim army survived but suffered a painful defeat that the Quran addressed directly (Surah Al Imran, 3:152-155). Khalid's role in this is recorded by Ibn Hisham and al-Tabari.

He accepted Islam in the eighth year after the Hijrah (8 AH / 629 CE), coming to Madinah with Amr ibn al-As and Uthman ibn Talhah. When they entered the presence of the Prophet ﷺ and took the shahada, the Prophet ﷺ said to Khalid: 'I knew you had reason within you and hoped that it would lead you to nothing but good.' (Ibn Hisham, al-Seerah al-Nabawiyyah). His conversion — accompanied by a request for forgiveness for his past actions against Islam — was accepted by the Prophet ﷺ with great warmth.

Khalid's first military engagement as a Muslim was the Expedition of Mu'tah (8 AH / 629 CE) — a campaign to the region of modern-day Jordan against a Byzantine-backed force. Three commanders were killed in succession: Zayd ibn Harithah, Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, and Abdullah ibn Rawahah, all of whom had been designated by the Prophet ﷺ in that order of succession. The Muslim army of approximately 3,000 men faced a Byzantine force recorded by classical historians as significantly larger. With the command in disarray and the force in danger of being annihilated, Khalid took the banner by the consensus of the men present and conducted a fighting withdrawal so skillfully that the army extricated itself with minimal further losses. When the army returned to Madinah, the Prophet ﷺ announced their survival and said: 'Khalid is a sword of Allah which He has unsheathed against the unbelievers.' (Sahih al-Bukhari, Kitab al-Maghazi — though the attribution of the title Sayf Allah to this specific occasion is recorded in various Seerah sources including Ibn Sa'd and Ibn Kathir)

In the following campaigns, Khalid became the primary military instrument of Muslim expansion. He commanded the vanguard in the Conquest of Makkah (8 AH), where he led the southern column and overcame the only armed resistance offered by Qurayshi fighters loyal to Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl and Safwan ibn Umayyah. He participated in the Battle of Hunayn (8 AH) against the Hawazin and Thaqif confederacy — one of the largest battles of the Prophet's era.

After the Prophet's death ﷺ, Khalid's role during Abu Bakr's caliphate was decisive. He was the primary commander in the ridda (apostasy) wars, personally defeating the forces of the false prophet Musaylimah al-Kadhdhab at the Battle of Yamama (11 AH / 633 CE) — the bloodiest battle in the Muslim world to that point, in which many hafizun (Quran memorizers) were martyred. He then turned the Muslim forces toward Iraq, where he defeated Sassanid Persian forces in a series of engagements along the Euphrates, including the battles of al-Ubullah, al-Walajah, Ullays, and al-Hira. He then received a letter from Abu Bakr ordering him to march to Syria where Muslim forces were struggling against Byzantine armies.

His forced march from Iraq to Syria is regarded by military historians as a logistical achievement of extraordinary difficulty — crossing the waterless Syrian desert in a route considered impassable. He arrived in Syria, assumed overall command of the Muslim armies, and united the four separate forces that had been operating in different parts of Syria under Abu Ubaydah, Amr ibn al-As, Shurahbil ibn Hasanah, and Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan. He then engineered the victory at the Battle of Ajnadayn (13 AH / 634 CE), one of the pivotal battles of early Islamic history.

The most celebrated of his Syrian campaigns was the Battle of al-Yarmuk (15 AH / 636 CE), fought against the largest Byzantine force the Muslims had faced — estimates in classical sources range from 100,000 to 200,000 Byzantine and allied troops against a Muslim force of approximately 25,000–40,000 (exact numbers in classical sources vary considerably). The battle lasted six days; Khalid's tactical genius — particularly his reorganization of the Muslim army into an elastic defensive formation on the fifth day when a Byzantine breakthrough nearly succeeded, and his decisive cavalry flanking maneuver on the sixth day — produced one of the most significant military victories in history. The Byzantine loss at Yarmuk effectively ended Byzantine control over greater Syria.

Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA), on becoming Caliph after Abu Bakr's death (13 AH), removed Khalid from supreme command in Syria and placed Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah in command — a decision that has been analyzed by classical scholars in various ways, with most agreeing that Umar was concerned about Muslims attributing victories to Khalid personally rather than to Allah's aid, and about maintaining the principle of command accountability. Khalid accepted the decision with full obedience. He continued to serve under Abu Ubaydah as a regular commander until the conclusion of the Syrian campaigns.

Khalid ibn al-Walid died in 21 AH (642 CE) in Hims (Homs), Syria, of natural causes. His death — in a bed rather than on the battlefield — was something he had expected and hoped would not be his fate. He reportedly said at his deathbed: 'I have fought in so many battles seeking martyrdom and it did not come to me. And now I die in my bed as animals die. Let there be no sleep in the eyes of cowards.' (Various Seerah sources; Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wal-Nihayah, Vol. 7). His body reportedly bore over eighty scars from swords, spears, and arrows received in battle.

The Prophet ﷺ said of him: 'Among the best of Allah's servants is Khalid ibn al-Walid — a sword among the swords of Allah.' (Musnad Ahmad; similar versions in various hadith collections). His military record, which classical historians record as approximately 100 battles and engagements without defeat, is unparalleled in early Islamic history.

key_events.event: Led Qurayshi cavalry flanking maneuver at Uhud — before his Islam
Accepted Islam in Madinah; Prophet ﷺ gave him the title Sayf Allah al-Maslul
Commanded the Muslim force at Mu'tah; saved the army after three commanders fell
Led the southern column in the Conquest of Makkah
Fought at the Battle of Hunayn
Battle of Yamama — defeated Musaylimah al-Kadhdhab and the ridda forces
Defeated Sassanid Persian forces along the Euphrates in multiple engagements
Forced march from Iraq to Syria; Battle of Ajnadayn — first major Syrian victory
Battle of al-Yarmuk — defeated Byzantine forces; Syria opened to Islam
Died of natural causes in Hims, Syria

notable_traits: Unparalleled tactical genius — never defeated in over a hundred engagements
Extreme personal courage — bore over eighty battle wounds
Rapid adaptation of strategy and formation under battlefield conditions
Full obedience to Caliph Umar's decision to relieve him of command — accepted without bitterness
Deep personal humility regarding his military gifts — attributed all success to Allah

key_relationships.father: al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah (one of the leading men of Quraysh)
key_relationships.brother: al-Walid ibn al-Walid (who accepted Islam at Badr and died a Muslim)
spouses: Multiple marriages recorded; Asma bint Anas ibn Mudrik among the named

narrated_hadith_count: approximately 18 hadith in the major collections
sources: Musnad Ahmad ibn Hanbal — Khalid narrations
al-Waqidi, al-Maghazi (with caution — al-Waqidi's reliability is debated by hadith scholars)
